title: Bartolomeo Cristofori and the first pianos (Florence, around 1700)

facts.text: Before the piano, the two stringed keyboard instruments were the clavichord and the harpsichord, used from about the 14th century until about 1800.
In a clavichord, a small metal blade (tangent) strikes the strings and keeps pressing them, so the sound is very quiet.
A clavichord player can make notes softer or louder by touch, but it is too quiet to accompany singers or play with other instruments.
A harpsichord plucks its strings with small plectra carried on jacks, so hitting a key harder does not change the volume much.
Even so, the harpsichord was the only stringed keyboard instrument loud enough for ensemble playing, and much fine music was written for it.
Bartolomeo Cristofori was a harpsichord maker in Florence who looked after the musical instruments of Prince Ferdinando de' Medici.
Cristofori began work on his new instrument in about 1698, shortly before 1700.
He set out to improve the harpsichord and ended up creating a new instrument.
He called it gravicembalo col piano e forte, Italian for a harpsichord with soft and loud; pianoforte and piano come from this name.
Cristofori replaced the plucking jacks with leather-covered wooden hammers that strike pairs of strings.
Because the hammer hits the string, pressing a key harder gives a louder note and pressing it gently gives a softer one.
His escapement lets the hammer fall away right after striking so the string keeps ringing; a check stops the hammer bouncing back.
Dampers rest on the strings and lift while a key is held down, then fall back to stop the sound when it is released.
The basic principles of Cristofori's action are still used in modern pianos.
An Italian journalist visited Cristofori's workshop in 1709 and two years later (1711) published an article praising the instruments.
The new instrument drew little notice in Italy; in 1732 L. Giustini of Pistoia published twelve sonatas for it, the first printed piano music.
Cristofori's design did not spread widely at first, and composers such as Domenico Scarlatti kept writing for the harpsichord.
Three of Cristofori's pianos survive: in New York (Metropolitan Museum of Art), Rome and Leipzig; the Leipzig one dates from 1726.
The Met's Cristofori piano, made in 1720, is described as the world's oldest surviving piano.
In Germany, organ maker Gottfried Silbermann probably learned of the design from a German translation of the 1711 article.
Silbermann showed his first pianos to J. S. Bach in 1736, but Bach criticized them; about ten years later Silbermann made an improved version.
Pianos did not come into general use until composers wanted bigger, louder sounds; Mozart, Haydn and Beethoven wrote for the pianoforte later in the 18th century.
As concerts moved from palaces into large public halls, the quieter harpsichord became less useful.
In 1768 J. C. Bach gave the first public solo piano recital in London, on a small square piano made by Johannes Zumpe.
Derived from the dates above: the first printed piano music (1732) appeared more than 30 years after Cristofori began his work (about 1698).
Pianos later grew much heavier and louder; by Beethoven's time they had double and triple strings on massive frames carrying roughly eighteen-ton loads.
